The wire is already extended by a force of 60 N.
How much work is done to increase the extension of the wire by 2.0 mm?
A
0.040 J
B
0.090 J
C
0.16 J
D
0.25 J

hints: Find the starting extension on the graph where force / N is 60: read across to the line then down to extension / $10^{-3} \text{ m}$.
Recall work done on the wire is the area under the force-extension graph, so the extra $2.0 \text{ mm}$ is a narrow strip starting from that stretched position, not from zero.
Treat that strip as a trapezium between $60 \text{ N}$ and the new higher force over width $2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$ and use area $= \frac{(F_1+F_2)}{2} \times \Delta x$.
walkthrough: Read the starting point from the straight-line graph. $F_1 = 60 \text{ N}$ meets the line at extension $x_1 = 3.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$.
Add the extra stretch $\Delta x = 2.0 \text{ mm} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$ to get the final extension $x_2 = 3.0 \times 10^{-3} + 2.0 \times 10^{-3} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$.
Read the final force at $x_2$ from the graph. At $5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$ the line reaches $F_2 = 100 \text{ N}$.
Work done is the area under the $F$-$x$ graph between $x_1$ and $x_2$. Because $F$ rises linearly, the strip is a trapezium: $W = \frac{(F_1 + F_2)}{2} \times \Delta x$.
This matches $0.16 \text{ J}$. This is option C

A.explanation: This is too small because it uses only the extra $2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$ with a low average force, ignoring that the force is already $60 \text{ N}$ and rising.

B.explanation: This is the work from zero to about $3.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$, not the extra strip of area when the wire is already stretched by $60 \text{ N}$.

C.explanation: The area under the graph from $3.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$ to $5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$ with forces $60 \text{ N}$ to $100 \text{ N}$ is $0.16 \text{ J}$.

D.explanation: This is the total elastic energy to $5.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$ at $100 \text{ N}$, not the additional work from the already stretched position.
